comparison: Perfect agreement on methodological claims (C1, C2, C75-C80). Both evaluations strongly support the experimental design, with OpenEval noting 'comprehensive methodological details' and peer reviewers calling it 'extremely clever' and 'careful.'

Strong agreement on core findings (C3-C8), though peer review also includes summary claims (C59-C62). Both find the dissociation between motor and perceptual biases well-supported. OpenEval emphasizes quantitative evidence while peer reviewers call it 'of fundamental significance.'

Strong agreement on PT-dependent dissociation (C14, C21, C23-C25, C27). OpenEval highlights tachometric curve analyses with statistical controls; peer reviewers specifically praised the 'dichotomy in choice performance' and 'rigorous analyses.' Peer review excludes C28 which appears in their R4.

Strong agreement on temporal characterization of biases (C22, C29-C36). OpenEval emphasizes systematic analysis with confidence intervals; peer reviewers found results 'clear' and 'consistent with prior literature.' Peer review also includes C28 not in OpenEval R4.

Perfect agreement on outcome-dependent modulation (C37-C43). Both support the findings, though OpenEval notes the interpretation of non-strategic behavior (C41-C42) is 'inferential' and could benefit from validation. Peer reviewers found evidence 'compelling' without raising this concern.

Strong agreement on statistical independence (C44-C48). OpenEval includes C62 while peer review does not. Both praise the sophisticated analysis; OpenEval emphasizes 'sound mathematical framework' while peer reviewers highlight 'potentially independent effects' as fundamental contribution.

Perfect agreement on cross-subject consistency (C49-C54). Both evaluations support the findings without concerns. OpenEval notes consistency in accuracy contrasts with RT variability; peer reviewers emphasize this strengthens generalizability.

Perfect agreement on task difficulty claims (C16-C20). Both accept the interpretation that randomization increases difficulty. OpenEval provides detailed statistical support; peer reviewers implicitly accept by noting consistency with prior literature.

Partial overlap on summary claims (C58-C61). OpenEval R9 focuses on high-level summary of main findings; peer R2 includes these claims alongside core findings (C3-C8). Both strongly support, with peer reviewers calling it 'fundamental.'

Partial overlap on contextualization claims. OpenEval R10 covers C63-C65 (task-dependent expression); peer R10 covers broader mechanistic interpretation (C58, C63-C70). Both find interpretations reasonable and consistent with literature, though OpenEval notes some speculation.

Strong agreement on priming mechanisms (C66-C70). OpenEval emphasizes extensive citations and neural explanations; peer reviewers explicitly state results are 'logical and consistent with prior literature,' supporting these mechanistic interpretations.

Perfect agreement on broader significance claims (C71-C74). Both strongly support the interpretation of real-world relevance and underappreciated magnitude of history effects. Peer reviewers emphasize 'fundamental significance' matching OpenEval's assessment.

Perfect agreement on tachometric methodology (C55-C57). Both accept the established methodology without challenge. OpenEval cites prior validation studies; peer reviewers praise the 'careful analysis' enabled by this approach.

Perfect agreement on background/definitional claims (C9-C13). Both evaluations support these as appropriate context from established literature. Peer reviewers implicitly accept by noting work 'broadens the framework' for understanding choice behavior.
